q: What is the defining characteristic of a sequence model compared with a model that treats inputs as an unordered collection?
options: It can model dependencies between elements according to their sequence positions
It requires every input to have exactly the same value
It can only process numerical features
It does not require training data
explanation: Sequence models are designed to capture relationships and dependencies among elements where order matters, such as words in a sentence or time-series observations.

q: What does an autoregressive model use to predict the next element in a sequence?
options: Only the final element of the training dataset
Previously observed elements in the sequence
Only randomly generated latent variables
The complete future sequence
explanation: An autoregressive model predicts the next element using previously observed elements, typically modeling the conditional probability of the next token given earlier tokens.

q: Which factorization best represents an autoregressive model for a sequence x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ?
options: p(x₁,...,xₙ) = ∏ᵢ p(xᵢ | x₁,...,xᵢ₋₁)
p(x₁,...,xₙ) = ∑ᵢ p(xᵢ)
p(x₁,...,xₙ) = ∏ᵢ p(xᵢ) only
p(x₁,...,xₙ) = p(xₙ | x₁) only
explanation: The autoregressive factorization decomposes the joint probability into conditional probabilities, where each element is predicted given all preceding elements.

q: What is the main purpose of a latent variable in a latent variable model?
options: To represent hidden factors that help explain observed data
To replace every observed feature with a label
To guarantee that the input sequence has no noise
To store the training dataset directly
explanation: Latent variables represent underlying or unobserved factors that can capture useful structure in the observed data.

q: What is the key mechanism that allows a basic RNN to process a sequence step by step?
options: A hidden state that is carried from one time step to the next
A separate unrelated model for every token
A fixed output that never changes with time
A convolution applied only once to the entire dataset
explanation: An RNN maintains a hidden state that is updated at each time step, allowing information from earlier elements to influence later computations.

q: In a basic RNN, what is the primary role of the hidden state?
options: To summarize relevant information from the sequence processed so far
To permanently store every training example
To convert all tokens into one-hot vectors
To calculate the optimizer learning rate
explanation: The hidden state acts as a running representation of information from previous time steps and is updated as new inputs are processed.

q: Why can a basic RNN struggle to learn long-range dependencies?
options: Repeated multiplication through time can cause vanishing or exploding gradients
RNNs cannot process more than one token
RNNs always use a non-differentiable step function
The hidden state is never updated
explanation: During backpropagation through time, gradients pass through many recurrent steps. Repeated multiplication can make gradients become extremely small or large.

q: What is tokenisation in natural language processing?
options: Converting text into smaller units such as words, subwords, or characters
Converting every sentence directly into a class label
Removing all numerical values from text
Training an RNN without input data
explanation: Tokenisation divides text into processing units called tokens. Depending on the tokenizer, tokens may represent words, subwords, characters, or other text units.

q: Why are subword tokens often useful in NLP?
options: They can represent unseen or rare words through reusable smaller units
They guarantee that every sentence has exactly one token
They eliminate the need for embeddings
They ensure every word has a unique character
explanation: Subword tokenisation can represent rare or unseen words by combining known subword units, helping reduce out-of-vocabulary problems.

q: What is the main purpose of a word embedding?
options: To represent words as dense numerical vectors that can capture semantic relationships
To assign every word a unique binary class label
To remove word order from every sequence
To convert every word into an image
explanation: Word embeddings map words to dense vectors. Words used in similar contexts often have related vector representations.

q: What does the distributional hypothesis underlying word embeddings suggest?
options: Words appearing in similar contexts tend to have related meanings
Every word must have a unique spelling
Word meaning is independent of surrounding words
Only word frequency determines meaning
explanation: The distributional hypothesis motivates learning word meaning from context: words occurring in similar contexts tend to acquire similar representations.

q: In Word2Vec, what is the main distinction between the CBOW and Skip-gram objectives?
options: CBOW predicts a target word from context, while Skip-gram predicts context words from a target word
CBOW uses characters while Skip-gram uses images
CBOW is autoregressive while Skip-gram cannot use text
CBOW produces probabilities while Skip-gram produces only labels
explanation: CBOW uses surrounding context to predict the target word. Skip-gram uses a target word to predict words occurring in its context.

q: What is one important property of Word2Vec embeddings?
options: They can learn useful relationships between words from their contexts
They require every word to have exactly the same meaning
They encode every sentence using only one scalar
They do not require a training corpus
explanation: Word2Vec learns word vectors from context relationships, allowing semantic and syntactic regularities to emerge in the embedding space.

q: How does GloVe primarily learn word representations?
options: By using global word co-occurrence statistics
By predicting image pixels from words
By randomly assigning vectors without training
By using only the first word of each sentence
explanation: GloVe, or Global Vectors, learns embeddings using statistics of word-word co-occurrences across a corpus.

q: What is a major difference between Word2Vec and GloVe?
options: Word2Vec is based on predictive context objectives, while GloVe explicitly uses global co-occurrence statistics
Word2Vec produces images while GloVe produces audio
Word2Vec cannot learn embeddings while GloVe can
GloVe requires no corpus while Word2Vec does
explanation: Word2Vec learns embeddings through predictive objectives such as CBOW or Skip-gram, whereas GloVe uses global word co-occurrence information.

q: What is the main motivation for LSTM networks compared with basic RNNs?
options: To better preserve and control information over long sequences
To eliminate all trainable parameters
To make every sequence independent of its previous elements
To replace tokenisation
explanation: LSTMs introduce a memory cell and gates that help control what information is retained, added, and discarded, improving learning of long-range dependencies.

q: Which set correctly identifies the main gates in a standard LSTM?
options: Input, forget, and output gates
Query, key, and value gates
Encode, decode, and classify gates
Token, word, and sentence gates
explanation: A standard LSTM uses input, forget, and output gates to regulate information entering the cell, information retained in the cell, and information exposed through the hidden state.

q: What is the main role of the forget gate in an LSTM?
options: To control how much previous cell-state information is retained
To calculate word-token boundaries
To convert attention scores into embeddings
To generate the final vocabulary
explanation: The forget gate produces values that control which information from the previous cell state should be retained or discarded.

q: What is the key idea behind a GRU?
options: It uses gating mechanisms to control information flow with a simpler structure than an LSTM
It removes the recurrent hidden state entirely
It requires a separate vocabulary for every time step
It uses only convolutional filters
explanation: A GRU is a gated recurrent architecture designed to capture dependencies over time while using a simpler gating structure than an LSTM.

q: Which statement best compares a standard LSTM and GRU?
options: An LSTM has a separate cell state, while a GRU combines its recurrent memory into a hidden state
A GRU has no trainable parameters, while an LSTM does
An LSTM cannot process sequences, while a GRU can
Both architectures are identical in their state structure
explanation: A standard LSTM maintains both a cell state and hidden state. A GRU uses a simpler architecture in which its hidden state serves as the main recurrent memory.

q: What is the main purpose of attention in sequence models?
options: To allow a model to focus on different parts of the input when producing a representation or output
To force every input token to have equal importance
To remove all contextual information
To replace the vocabulary with numerical labels
explanation: Attention computes weights over relevant representations so the model can emphasize different input elements depending on the current task or query.

q: In scaled dot-product attention, what are Q, K, and V?
options: Query, Key, and Value
Question, Kernel, and Vector
Query, Knowledge, and Vocabulary
Quantization, Keyframe, and Value
explanation: Q, K, and V stand for Query, Key, and Value. Queries and keys determine attention compatibility, while values provide the information that is combined.

q: Which sequence correctly describes scaled dot-product attention?
options: Compute QKᵀ, scale the scores, apply softmax, then take a weighted sum of V
Apply softmax to V, then multiply Q by K without scaling
Multiply Q and V, apply sigmoid, then add K
Tokenise V, concatenate Q and K, then apply ReLU
explanation: Scaled dot-product attention computes query-key compatibility, scales the scores, converts them to attention weights with softmax, and uses those weights to combine the value vectors.

q: Why is the dot product in scaled dot-product attention divided by the square root of the key dimension?
options: To control the magnitude of attention scores and help keep softmax gradients well behaved
To convert every key into a probability
To remove the need for softmax
To ensure all value vectors become zero
explanation: Scaling by the square root of the key dimension helps prevent dot-product scores from becoming excessively large, which can make softmax overly peaked and gradients less useful.

q: What is self-attention?
options: Attention where queries, keys, and values are derived from the same sequence representation
Attention where only the labels are used as keys
Attention that can only operate on a single token
Attention that requires a separate model for each word
explanation: In self-attention, Q, K, and V are generated from the same input sequence, allowing each token to relate to other tokens in that sequence.

q: What is cross-attention?
options: Attention where queries come from one sequence or representation and keys and values come from another
Attention where Q, K, and V must all come from the same token
Attention that ignores the values
Attention used only for tokenisation
explanation: Cross-attention connects two representations: queries are produced from one source, while keys and values are obtained from another source.

q: What is causal or masked self-attention designed to prevent during autoregressive generation?
options: A position from attending to future positions that are not yet available
A position from attending to itself
The model from using any previous token
The model from computing attention weights
explanation: Causal masking prevents each position from accessing future tokens, preserving the autoregressive property needed for left-to-right generation.

q: What is the main purpose of multi-head attention?
options: To allow the model to learn different attention patterns in parallel representation subspaces
To reduce every sequence to one token before attention
To eliminate all projection matrices
To make attention independent of the input
explanation: Multi-head attention uses multiple attention heads, enabling the model to learn different relationships or patterns in different representation subspaces.

q: Why does a sequence model typically need positional information when using self-attention?
options: Self-attention alone does not inherently encode the order of tokens
Self-attention cannot process numerical vectors
Positional information replaces token embeddings completely
Positional information is required only for word2vec
explanation: Self-attention compares token representations without inherently distinguishing their positions. Positional information provides the model with sequence-order information.

q: In attention, what does a high attention weight between a query and a particular key indicate?
options: The corresponding value is given relatively greater influence in the output
The key is removed from the sequence
The query becomes a new vocabulary token
The value is guaranteed to be the correct class label
explanation: Attention weights determine how strongly each value contributes to the weighted sum. A higher weight gives the corresponding value greater influence.
